..
Issued at 200 PM CST Sat Nov 14 2026

With an omega blocking pattern over the central CONUS, mild and
dry weather continues across western and central North Dakota. 
Breezy south to southeasterly winds, sustained around 15 to 20 
MPH and gusting up to 35 MPH, have developed across much of the 
area due to the tightening of the surface pressure gradient 
between a surface high over northern Minnesota and a low center 
spit out into Montana by lee cyclogenesis over the northern 
Rockies. Partly cloudy skies will persist across the area as low
to mid level moistures continues to stream northward across the
Great Plains. Highs this afternoon are forecast from the lower 
40s east to the mid 50s west. With winds becoming very light
across western North Dakota this evening and overnight, patchy
fog is possible along the ND/MT border late tonight through
Sunday morning. 

Late tonight into Sunday, a Pacific Trough is progged to be 
rapidly subsumed into the general northwesterly flow over the 
southern Canadian Prairies, ejecting a shortwave impulse that 
will held erode and eject the ridging portions of the omega 
block further to the east. The resulting southwesterly flow over
the northern Plains Sunday through the early portions of the 
next week will continue to promote mild and dry weather across 
the area, with highs broadly in the 50s and lows in the 30s each
day. With broad high pressure underneath the ridge situated 
over the eastern CONUS, and with ongoing lee cyclogenesis over 
the northern Rockies, a mild MSLP gradient will persist over 
eastern North Dakota, promoting somewhat breezy conditions over 
the south central Sunday and Monday, with sustained speeds 
around 10 to 15 MPH and gusts up to 25 MPH coming out of the 
south. Otherwise, quiet weather is anticipated through this 
period. 

Looking further head, a pattern shift is anticipated through 
the later half of the week as the influence of a deep Pacific 
Northwestern low increases across the northern Plains. On 
Wednesday, the ensemble advertises the arrival of an initial 
shortwave that the ensemble expects to spin up and loft a 
surface low pressure system across the northern Plains through 
Thursday morning. With this, low to medium chances (40 to 70 
percent) for precpitation can be anticipated across much of the 
forecast area. Cluster analysis indicates two potential tracks 
with this initial system. The faster, more northerly track is 
slightly favored (60 percent of ensemble members), which 
captures the low pressure system cutting slightly more directly 
across North Dakota into the southern Canadian Prairies. The 
shorter residence time over the forecast area would generally 
limit overall QPF Wednesday into Thursday, with most locations 
limited to around 0.1" or so. A slightly slower, more southerly 
track (40 percent of members) would maximize the residence time 
of precpitation over North Dakota Wednesday into Thursday, and 
would allow QPF to approach 0.25". While cooler air would also 
accompany this system, driving highs down into the 40s, rain is 
favored at this time. Some light snow may mix in with the rain 
across the north during the coolest hours of Thursday morning, 
though no accumulations are currently anticipated. 

Conditions are expected to briefly dry out late Thursday into 
early Friday behind this initial system, though chances for 
precpitation will again increase across the area through the day
Friday as the main Pacific wave crosses over the Rockies and 
slides across the northern Plains. Similar to Wednesday, cluster
analysis reveals two potential scenarios depending on the track
of the low. A more northerly route (60 percent of ensemble 
members) would allow for more cool air to be ingested in the 
system as it passes through the forecast area, and thus a 
transition from mostly rain on Friday into mostly snow by early 
Saturday would be anticipated. Snowfall accumulations across the
area of an inch or so could be anticipated, with a low chance 
for portions of the west into south central North Dakota to 
exceed 2 inches of snow by late Saturday into early Sunday. 
Highs in this scenario would mainly be in the 30s. The southerly
route (40 percent of members) instead has much of this 
precpitation fall as rain, with some snow beginning to mix in by
early Saturday morning. In this scenario, high temperatures in 
the upper 30s into the 40s would quickly erode whatever trace of
snowfall does end up falling Saturday morning. These clusters 
remain very poorly dispersed at this timeframe, with scenario 1 
being mainly a combination of the GEPS and the GEFs, while 
scenario 2 is mainly the ENS.
